specPoints.text: know the definition of standard enthalpy change of: i reaction, ∆ r H ii formation, ∆ f H iii combustion, ∆ c H iv neutralisation, ∆ neut H v atomisation, ∆ at H

primer.text: Five standard enthalpy changes anchor the energetics chapter: reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation and atomisation. Each definition fixes the substance, the quantity of one mole and the standard conditions. This note states all five, writes the matching equations, and shows why an element in its standard state scores zero.

lessons.title: The five standard enthalpy definitions
lessons.opening: Five definitions anchor the energetics chapter, and each one hides three marks: the substance, the quantity of one mole, and the standard conditions. Learn them as a family - reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation and atomisation - and read the precision each demands.
keyPoints: Standard conditions are 100 kPa pressure and 298 K, with every substance in its standard state.
The standard enthalpy change of reaction is the enthalpy change for the equation's stated amounts.
The standard enthalpy change of formation is the change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements.
The standard enthalpy change of combustion is the change when one mole burns completely in oxygen.
Neutralisation gives one mole of water; atomisation gives one mole of gaseous atoms from the element.

low.restatement: Five labels, one template: state the substance, fix the quantity at one mole (except the general reaction change), and pin the standard conditions of 100 kPa and 298 K.
low.analogy: Five passport photos of the same idea: the face (substance) changes, the frame (one mole, standard conditions) never does.
low.examPointer: Losing the word 'standard' or the 'one mole' phrase is how most definition marks die - write both into every definition.

medium.restatement: The definitions are equation-generating machines: formation demands elements in standard states making exactly one mole of product; combustion demands complete oxidation to CO2 and H2O; atomisation demands free gaseous atoms - each constraint writes the equation for you.
medium.analogy: Each definition is a fill-in-the-blank template; the blanks (states, coefficients) are where the marks hide.
medium.examPointer: Write the equation beside the definition when asked - a definition without its balanced equation earns only half the available credit.

check.stem: Which conditions define a STANDARD enthalpy change?

options.explanation: The standard pair, quoted every time.
273 K is freezing point, not the standard temperature.

options.text: 1 atm and 25 degrees only for gases
options.explanation: The conditions bind every substance.
Standard means the fixed reference pair.

check.stem: The standard enthalpy change of formation produces how much product?

options.text: Exactly one mole of the compound
options.explanation: One mole is built into the definition.
That describes the reaction change, not formation.
Mass units never appear in the definition.
One mole of the compound, not of atoms.

options.text: The standard enthalpy change of combustion
options.explanation: Complete burning in oxygen under standard conditions.

options.text: The standard enthalpy change of formation
options.explanation: Formation builds from elements.

options.text: The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation
options.explanation: Neutralisation makes water.

options.text: The standard enthalpy change of atomisation
options.explanation: Atomisation makes gaseous atoms.

check.stem: What does the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation count?

options.explanation: The neutralisation definition fixes water's quantity.
The acid amount varies with stoichiometry.
Salt stoichiometry varies; water does not.
No hydrogen gas forms in neutralisation.

check.stem: What does the standard enthalpy change of atomisation deliver?

options.text: One mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state
options.explanation: The element is dismantled into free gaseous atoms.
Atoms, not molecules.

options.text: One mole of ions in solution
options.explanation: Ions belong to solution chemistry.

options.text: One mole of compound from atoms
options.explanation: That inverts the formation direction.

check.stem: State the standard enthalpy change of formation definition in full.
check.modelAnswer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions of 100 kPa and 298 K.

check.stem: List the five standard enthalpy changes by name.
check.modelAnswer: Reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation and atomisation.

check.stem: Explain why states of matter must be specified in these definitions.
check.modelAnswer: Enthalpy depends on the physical state - gas, liquid or solid hold different energy contents - so an unstated state leaves the defined quantity ambiguous.

check.stem: Write the standard formation equation for ammonia, NH3(g), and state the standard conditions that apply to it.
check.modelAnswer: (1/2)N2(g) + (3/2)H2(g) -> NH3(g), quoted at 100 kPa and 298 K with every species gaseous in its standard state.

lessons.title: The definitions table in use
lessons.opening: The definitions earn their keep when converted into equations. Two conventions run the table: an element in its standard state carries zero formation enthalpy, and every formation equation balances to exactly one mole of product.
keyPoints: An element in its standard state has a standard enthalpy change of formation of zero.
Formation equations must balance to exactly one mole of the compound on the product side.
Fractional coefficients on the elements are permitted to reach the one-mole target.
Combustion equations send one mole of fuel to CO2 and H2O with states shown.
Reading the definitions table means converting each row into its balanced, state-specified equation.

low.restatement: Elements in their normal state score zero; formation equations balance to one mole of product even if that needs fractions like half a molecule of oxygen.
low.analogy: The zero is the reference floor of the energy ladder, and the one-mole rule is the ladder's fixed rung spacing.
low.examPointer: Do not clear fractions to whole numbers in formation equations - the one-mole product overrides the no-fractions habit from other topics.

medium.restatement: The zero convention exists because the ladder needs a floor: measuring formation relative to elements removes arbitrary absolute energies and makes cycles additive - every later Hess calculation stands on this floor.
medium.analogy: Sea level is the zero for mountains; elements in standard states are the sea level of enthalpy.
medium.examPointer: Write state symbols in every equation from the table - the state symbols are part of the definition's precision and carry marks.

check.stem: What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of oxygen gas, O2(g)?

options.text: Zero, because it is an element in its standard state
options.explanation: The reference floor applies.
Only compounds carry non-zero formation values.
Elements are the floor, not a cost.
The convention defines it exactly.

check.stem: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol, C2H5OH(l)?

options.explanation: Elements in standard states balancing to one mole of product.
Two moles of product break the one-mole rule.
That is decomposition, reversed.
The reactant must be elements, not a compound.

check.stem: Why are fractional coefficients acceptable in formation equations?

options.text: The one-mole product rule forces them when element counts are odd
options.explanation: The product quantity outranks the whole-number habit.
Coefficients do not affect energy meaning.
The convention is functional, not aesthetic.
The one-mole rule demands them.

check.stem: What must accompany every equation quoted from the definitions table?

options.explanation: States are part of the definition's precision.
Definitions do not involve catalysts.
The standard conditions are quoted, not drawn.
State symbols are required.

check.stem: The combustion definition sends one mole of fuel to which products under standard conditions?

options.text: CO2(g) and H2O(l), complete burning in excess oxygen
options.explanation: The complete-oxidation pair.
Carbon monoxide marks incomplete burning.
That is decomposition, not combustion.
Hydrogen gas is not a combustion product.

check.stem: State why an element's standard formation enthalpy is zero.
check.modelAnswer: Elements in their standard states are the reference floor from which all formation enthalpies are measured, so their own formation change is zero by definition.

check.stem: Write the formation equation for methanol, CH3OH(l), from its elements.
check.modelAnswer: C(s) + 2H2(g) + (1/2)O2(g) -> CH3OH(l), with every element in its standard state and one mole of product.

check.stem: Explain why the one-mole product rule matters when writing formation equations.
check.modelAnswer: Formation enthalpies feed Hess cycles as per-mole quantities, so an equation making two moles would deliver the wrong scale into every cycle built on it - the rule keeps the table additive.

check.stem: Write the standard formation equation for propan-1-ol, C3H7OH(l), and verify the hydrogen count.
check.modelAnswer: 3C(s) + 4H2(g) + (1/2)O2(g) -> C3H7OH(l): the elements' hydrogens total 4 x 2 = 8, matching the product's 7 + 1 = 8 hydrogens.

glossary.definition: The reference conditions of 100 kPa and 298 K under which standard enthalpy changes are quoted.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
The enthalpy change when one mole of water forms in an acid-base reaction.
